final_answer:
SHORT ANSWER. Yes, there is recourse, and the order of operations matters: (1) first file, with the immigration court, a motion to reopen and rescind the August 1, 2025 in absentia removal order based on lack of notice (INA 240(b)(5)(C)(ii)); no filing fee is required for that motion; (2) if it is granted, pursue the USCIS denials (I-130 and I-485) through USCIS motions and/or renewal of adjustment before the immigration judge.

1. IMMIGRATION COURT FILING (as of April 1, 2026). A written motion to reopen and rescind the in absentia order, filed with the immigration court that issued it (EOIR practice also uses a cover page and proof of service on DHS/ICE OPLA, and the motion should include an affidavit, evidence, and the proposed relief application). Because the argument is that he never received notice of the proceedings, the statute and 8 CFR 1003.23(b)(4)(ii) allow filing at any time; the 180-day exceptional-circumstances deadline (which expired about January 28, 2026) does not apply to a lack-of-notice motion. Under INA 240(b)(5)(A) an in absentia order requires that written notice was provided under 239(a)(1) or (2); under 240(b)(5)(C)(ii) the order may be rescinded if the alien demonstrates he did not receive notice in accordance with 239(a)(1) or (2). Filing the motion automatically stays removal pending the judge's decision (8 CFR 1003.23(b)(4)(ii)). Only one such motion is allowed. Include: a sworn declaration that the NTA address was never provided by him and that he never received any notice; evidence of his actual address(es) and of the address the couple gave USCIS (I-130/I-485 receipts, the wrong-address RFE and denial mailings, USCIS address records); proof that he and his wife believed the cases were pending (diligence, incentive to appear because he had a pending adjustment application); and the date he learned of the order (April 1, 2026) to show prompt action. Notice mailed to an address he never provided is not notice 'at the address provided' under INA 239(a)(1)(F)/(2); a presumption of delivery for regular mail applies only where the notice is properly addressed, and it can be rebutted with affidavits and other evidence (Matter of M-R-A-). Caution: Campos-Chaves v. Garland (2024) holds that a defective NTA is not itself enough if the respondent received a proper notice of hearing for the missed hearing; so the declaration must establish non-receipt of notice of the hearing as well, and that no notice reached him. Also confirm through the EOIR automated case system (1-800-898-7180 or the online portal) and the ROP/FOIA, whether the NTA was actually served and what address was used, and whether he was ever served in person. Recommend filing a change-of-address (EOIR-33/IC) with the motion. If the immigration court finds no notice, the order is rescinded and proceedings reopened (and the 10-year bar of INA 240(b)(7) on adjustment does not apply).

2. FEES. A motion to reopen based on lack of notice under INA 240(b)(5)(C)(ii) has no fee (8 CFR 1003.24(b)(2)(iii)), and DOJ's OBBBA fee guidance exempts these motions from the OBBBA fee. If instead the motion had to rest on exceptional circumstances or any other ground (outside the 180-day period, a fallback that would be hard to win), the ordinary motion-to-reopen fee is $145 plus the OBBBA motion fee ($900 in FY2025, adjusted for inflation to about $920 for FY2026; I could not open the primary sources to confirm the exact FY2026 figure), with a fee waiver largely restricted by OBBBA. Fees for later EOIR filings, such as an I-485 renewed before the judge or an appeal, should be checked at the time; new EOIR fees are reported to start October 1, 2026. Treat the amounts other than 'no fee' as unverified.

3. THE I-130 AND I-485 DENIALS. (a) The I-130 was denied as abandoned for failure to respond to the RFE; the abandonment denial cannot be appealed, but the petitioner may file a motion to reopen (8 CFR 103.2(b)(15)) on Form I-290B under 8 CFR 103.5. The 30-day deadline long since passed, but USCIS may excuse a late motion to reopen if the delay was reasonable and beyond the filer's control (8 CFR 103.5(a)(1)(i)); non-receipt of an RFE and decision sent to an address the couple never gave is a strong basis, together with evidence that they never received either. (b) The I-485 denial is not appealable; it is without prejudice to renewal in removal proceedings (8 CFR 245.2(a)(5)(ii)). Once proceedings are reopened, he can renew adjustment before the immigration judge, but that needs an approved or approvable I-130 (the court can adjudicate a visa petition in certain circumstances; alternatively USCIS reopens the I-130 and files a fresh I-130 if needed). A new I-130 plus I-485 is also possible, and as spouse of a citizen he is an immediate relative, who ordinarily is not barred by overstay or unauthorized-status grounds under INA 245(c), but this must be analysed. (c) Risks: marriage 19 days after a B-2 entry raises a possible misrepresentation or preconceived-intent issue (State Department 90-day rule guidance), and the marriage must be bona fide.

UNRESOLVED. I could not open primary sources for the statute, CFR text, or the EOIR fee notices (access blocked), so statutory and regulatory propositions rest on search results; verify before filing.
